newsitem.title: INDIA: Nuns to elect Mother Teresa's successor any day.
newsitem.headline: Nuns to elect Mother Teresa's successor any day.

text.p: More than 100 Roman Catholic nuns, closeted in secret deliberations for weeks, will elect a successor to Mother Teresa at the head of her religious order any day now, a senior church official said on Thursday.
"The deliberations have continued for over a month," Father Antony Rodrigues, secretary to the Archbishop of Calcutta, told Reuters in the eastern Indian city.
The 86-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner, suffering from heart, kidney and lung ailments, has said she does not want to continue to lead the Missionaries of Charity order which she founded in 1948.
She was sent to hospital three times last year, and although she continues to work, she has lost some of her characteristic vigour, church officials said.
The election of Mother Teresa's successor has been postponed twice since September. It was first set for September 8, but put off because Mother Teresa was ill.
A total of 132 senior nuns from around the world then went into retreat on January 16, confining themselves to their rooms in the order's headquarters in Calcutta for prayer.

They had planned to vote in a secret ballot on February 2, after the two-week retreat. But the order's electoral college, apparently unable to find a clear-cut successor for the charismatic Mother Teresa, decided instead to hold closed-door deliberations at the headquarters before holding a vote.
Earlier this week sources close to the religious order said the election process would be completed by March 15 because overseas delegates were booked on flights out of the country on the next day.
The sources said the order might opt to set up a committee of senior nuns to lead it rather than name one successor to Mother Teresa.
The 1979 Nobel Peace laureate, affectionately known as "Mother", had wanted to step down in 1990, a year after she was fitted with a heart pacemaker, but was persuaded to stay on.
She has led the order from the start, shaping the mission's work with her strong personality.

Church officials say none of the nuns who might succeed Mother Teresa can match her charisma, but several stand out for their experience, administrative ability and disciplined devotion to the order's taxing demands.
The election process involves the 132 members of the order's electoral order, or General Chapter, which represents the order's 4,500 nuns.
Three councillors-general -- Sisters Frederick, Joseph Michael and Priscilla Lewis -- and senior nuns Nirmala and Agnes Das, have long been considered front-runners.
But the 66-year-old Agnes Das, whom Mother Teresa has described as her "second self", was believed to be suffering from cancer.
